headline_insight: Just over half of clients report insurance reduced their financial stress (51.3% of women, 54.7% of men), but close to half — 47.1% of women and 43.2% of men — say it had no effect at all, and none of the gender or disability gaps in this section reach statistical significance after adjustment.
paragraphs: Insurance is delivering a real but partial dividend in financial resilience, and it is delivering it almost equally to women and men. Among the 1,518 female and 586 male clients answering, 21.5% of women and 23.5% of men said their financial stress was significantly reduced, with a further 29.8% and 31.2% respectively reporting some reduction. The mirror image is the more arresting number: 47.1% of women and 43.2% of men reported no effect on financial stress whatsoever, a 3.9 percentage point gap that is not statistically significant (p_adj = 0.3). Deterioration is rare in both groups — 1.5% of women and 2.0% of men reported stress increasing somewhat or significantly. The picture for households with a person with a disability is virtually identical: 22.2% of PWD households reported significant stress reduction against 22.1% of non-PWD households, and 47.8% versus 45.3% reported no effect, with every disability comparison in this section returning adjusted p-values of 0.5 or above. Benchmark data is not available for this indicator, so these levels should be read against VisionFund's own future rounds rather than an external standard.

Child wellbeing follows the same pattern of parity at a modest level. Just under a third of clients said cover had improved outcomes for the children they support — 31.9% of women and 32.6% of men, and 31.4% of PWD households against 32.4% of non-PWD households — while roughly 60% in every subgroup said it had not. Where improvements were reported, they clustered on daily functioning and health access rather than schooling: 16.5% of women and 17.7% of men cited children's ability to continue normal daily activities, and 15.1% and 17.4% cited improved access to healthcare treatment and diagnosis. The largest single gender gap in the child module is on fewer school days missed due to improved health (5.9% of women versus 9.2% of men, a 3.3 point difference), but this too falls short of significance once adjusted (p_adj = 0.1) and should be treated as directional.

The coping-behaviour data tells a quieter story that matters for product design. Reported use of harmful coping strategies is low across the board — 0.6% of women and 1.2% of men reduced food or essential spending, and 0.3% and 0.5% took children out of school — but men were consistently more likely to report the two liquidity-driven responses: borrowing money (9.7% versus 6.3%) and selling assets or livestock (3.2% versus 1.6%). Both differences carry adjusted p-values of 0.1 and are therefore directional rather than robust. Women, conversely, were slightly more likely to report closing a business temporarily (0.9% versus 0.3%) or an 'other' response (1.6% versus 0.5%), hinting that female clients may absorb shocks through their enterprise and informal networks rather than through formal borrowing — a hypothesis this survey can suggest but not confirm.

The verbatim responses from the small group who selected 'other' (24 women and 3 men, too few to generalise from) make that informality concrete. A female client in Malawi described a collective response: "We also contributed 1000 each to pay for our friend because she was admitted for over a month." A male client in Zambia said simply, "People helped me to do everything," while a female client in Rwanda reported, "I used my pocket money," and a female client in Tanzania pointed to a parallel scheme — "Nina bima ya NHIF." A female client in Uganda described using her loan to pay medical bills, which is a resilience response of last resort rather than a sign the insurance worked. Read alongside the near-50% 'no effect' finding, these voices suggest the binding constraint is not whether clients are covered but whether cover arrives fast enough and visibly enough to displace informal contributions, pocket money and loan diversion at the moment of shock. For programming, the priority is not a gender-differentiated product — the data offers no significant basis for one — but a universal improvement in claims speed, payout adequacy and client understanding of what the policy actually covers, with the male skew toward borrowing and asset sales monitored in the next round to see whether it hardens into a real pattern.
